newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma dismisses impact from U.S. travel ban.
newsitem.headline: Burma dismisses impact from U.S. travel ban.

text.p: A senior Burmese government official on Friday shrugged off a U.S. travel ban on Burmese leaders, saying it would have little effect as few government officials travelled to the United States.
"We are are not going to protest it as it does not jeopardise our national security and is diplomatic play," a senior government official told Reuters.
He said not many Burmese officials travel to the United States unless there was an urgent reason, so the travel ban would not have much impact.
"After all, relations are already pretty cool. So if they (the United States) don't want to deal with us, then we will deal with others who want to do so," he added.
U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday signed a proclamation banning Burma's military rulers and their families from entering the United States.
The ban was introduced as a response to "ongoing repression" of the democracy movement headed by Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) arrested hundreds of pro-democracy activists late last week to prevent a three-day meeting of Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) from being held at her house in Rangoon.

The travel ban comes just after Congress approved a Foreign Operations Appropriations bill that includes an ammendment allowing for possible sanctions against Burma because of its human rights record.
Burma recently accused the United States of colluding with Suu Kyi and helping her organise the party meeting, which the government says would have caused instability in the country.
"If they don't want positive interaction with us, it seems very strange that they should continue to maintain their embassy here," the Burmese official said.
